conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time for this. I’m Claire, a perinatal-mental-health specialist. Over the next few minutes I’d like to use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (the EPDS) to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply ten short questions about the past seven days; no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me you’re in danger. My goal is to understand how you’re coping so we can make sure you get whatever support you need. Ready to start?

First, how have you been able to enjoy things—little moments of laughter, music, a good cup of coffee—over the past week?

Honestly, Claire, most things feel kind of… flat. I can still smile when the baby grips my finger or when my partner makes a dumb joke, but that spark—where I used to feel a little rush of “this is great”—isn’t really there. Even my morning coffee, which used to feel like a treat, just tastes like something I need to keep my eyes open.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I still laugh sometimes—like when my sister sent that silly meme—but it feels kind of forced, like I’m reminding myself “this is funny, you should laugh.” Most days I don’t really find much funny at all; I’m too tired or just not in the mood.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. My mom keeps saying, “Let’s plan a coffee date,” or my partner asks if I want to stream our show after the baby’s down, but I can’t muster any real excitement. I say yes to be polite, but inside I’m just thinking, “What’s the point? I’ll still feel worn out.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes—like last night when she wouldn’t settle and I kept thinking maybe I’m not feeding her right, or I must’ve done something during the day to make her fussy. Rationally I know babies just cry, but the thought still pops in that it’s my fault she’s uncomfortable.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah, that happens. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my heart’s racing, sure something’s wrong with the baby—maybe her breathing sounds different or I think I missed a dirty diaper. Even if everything looks fine, I can’t shake the “what-if” loop in my head.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Once or twice this week, mostly at night. I’ll wake up to check on her and suddenly feel like the walls are closing in—my chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen even though she’s sleeping right there. It passes after a minute, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—most days, honestly. Between feedings, diaper changes, and trying to nap when she naps, it feels like the to-do list just grows longer while I’m stuck under it. I’ll look at the pile of laundry or the stack of unopened mail and think, “I’m drowning here,” but I can’t seem to start any of it.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not so much that I’m lying there miserable—more that my mind keeps spinning with little worries about the baby and all the stuff I didn’t finish. I’ll doze off, then jolt awake thinking I heard her cry. Most nights I’m awake two or three times for no real reason, and it takes forever to settle again.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel that way some of the time—like a gray cloud parked over my head. It isn’t constant, but every afternoon, when the baby finally naps and the house is quiet, this wave of sadness just sort of rolls in. I’ll sit there staring out the window feeling heavy and teary, even though nothing specific happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I got a little teary yesterday when I couldn’t get her to latch and my nipples were sore, but actual crying—like breaking down—hasn’t happened. Mostly the sadness just sits in my chest without spilling out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel overwhelmed and tired, but I would never want to hurt myself. My baby needs me, and I want to be here for her.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Reported Symptoms  
- Persistent low mood (“gray cloud”) most afternoons  
- Marked anhedonia—minimal enjoyment, forced laughter  
- Excessive guilt re infant care (“I must’ve done something wrong”)  
- Recurrent, unprovoked anxiety and nocturnal panic (racing heart, chest tightness, breathlessness)  
- Intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety  
- Sense of being overwhelmed/drowning in daily tasks  
- Initial insomnia and frequent nocturnal awakenings associated with ruminative worry  
- No current suicidal or self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)

Pattern  
Consistent with subsyndromal depressive and anxious symptoms emerging since delivery; functional impact moderate (sleep disruption, task avoidance).

Screening Significance  
Symptoms meet threshold for further evaluation for postpartum depression and anxiety; no immediate safety concerns identified. Recommend formal clinical assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and follow-up within 1–2 weeks.
